That number everyone worships. 125 percent net revenue retention. The signature of a great CS function, we say.

Here is what nobody says out loud.

No QBR produced it. No success plan produced it. No CSM ran a play that moved Snowflake from 118 to 125. Customers consume more compute because their own business generates more data. The pricing model is doing the retention. The meter is the motion.

That is not a slur on their CS team. It is a description of consumption economics.

And if it is true at the top of the market, it is true in your portfolio too.

Most CS orgs cannot tell the difference between the retention they caused and the retention they happened to be standing next to when the meter ticked up.

So they take credit for expansion they never touched. Then they get blindsided when a green account churns at renewal.

The dollar number lies. The usage velocity tells the truth first.

I break down the full decomposition, plus a free audit you can run Monday, in this week's issue.

Here is a test. Pull your ten biggest expansion accounts from the last year.

For each one, name the specific CS action that caused the growth. Not influenced. Caused.

The ones where you can name a documented play? That is earned retention. You own that.

The ones where you shrug and say the usage just went up? That is metered retention. The pricing model did it. You were standing next to the meter when it ticked.

Most CSMs cannot tell them apart. So the dashboard stays green while a metered account quietly stops consuming. The dollar number tells a lovely story right up until the day it doesn't.

That account did not churn at renewal. It churned in the usage graph three quarters earlier. The renewal was just the day you found out.

The meter reports churn last.

Watch usage velocity, not dollars, and you catch it while there is still time to act.

So here is my question for the CS leaders here: how many of your green accounts are already having their March, and you don't know it yet?

Consumption pricing broke your retention math. Here is how to fix it.

Five moves. Run them this week.

1. Decompose your biggest expansion account. Separate the usage growth a CS action caused from the usage growth that just happened. The migration that passed through the meter is not your win.

2. Label every green account as earned or metered. Earned means a documented CS play moved it. Metered means the customer workload moved it.

3. Switch your leading indicator from dollars to usage velocity. Dollars report churn last. Velocity reports it first.

4. Build the two-line board report before someone asks. Earned retention: CS caused this. Metered NRR: the pricing model caused this. Be honest about the split.

5. Take one metered account off your best CSM's heavy-touch list. It is riding the meter without them. Redeploy that attention to an account you can actually save.

The goal is not to shrink your numbers. It is to know which numbers you can defend when the meter turns against you.

I put a 118 percent account in a QBR deck once. Called it a win. Told the board the account team was driving growth.

Then I pulled the usage logs.

Most of that growth arrived in a single ten-week window in the spring. The customer had run a data migration off a legacy platform. Every record passed through the meter as ingest. Nobody on my side planned it, influenced it, or even knew it was happening until the invoice moved.

I took credit for a migration.

That stung. Because the flip side is what really hurt. If the meter can hand you expansion you never earned, it can hand you contraction you never see coming. And it does. Quietly. In the usage graph. Months before the dashboard goes red.

The accounts I felt best about were the ones I understood least.

The uncomfortable truth of consumption pricing is that a lot of your green is not yours. And the day you learn to subtract the meter from the motion is the day you find out how much retention you were actually earning.

Go earn the retention you keep taking credit for.
